idiom_name: hand-rolled capability table: type tag plus function-pointer struct (GObject type/interface query as the library route)
implementation_notes: C has neither interfaces nor run-time type information, so the query is data the program maintains itself: give every object a type or capability tag (an enum, a bitmask or a string id) and a table of function pointers, then write one query function that compares the requested capability id and returns the matching function pointer or NULL. What replaces the classic structure is this tag-and-table convention - the whole structure is hand-written, including the id registry and its versioning. The closest library-level analogue is GObject: g_type_is_a() answers whether a type conforms to an interface and g_type_interface_peek() returns the interface structure (NULL when the class does not conform), but that means adopting GLib's object system. Hand-rolling remains justified in kernels, embedded targets and plugin ABIs that cannot carry a GObject-sized runtime.
pitfalls: The query is a convention, not a guarantee: nothing in C checks that the returned function pointer has the signature the caller expects, so a mismatched capability id is undefined behaviour rather than a type error.

Capability ids as strings or as unversioned enums drift between a plugin and its host; use a stable numeric id and version the ops table so an object built against an older layout is detected instead of misread.

The function-pointer table must be the first member of the struct (or be reached through a documented accessor) so handles stay ABI-stable; reordering or padding the struct silently breaks every caller.
